summary: Route leaks in BGP have caused frequent significant disruptions, but there has been no common definition of the term. This informational RFC offers a working definition and classifies the kinds of route leaks seen in real incidents.

plainLanguage.summary: When one network tells another about a route it should not have passed on, the Internet can be sent the wrong way. This document says what counts as a route leak, and sorts the kinds that have caused real outages into six types, each with the incidents that fit it.

questions: what is a bgp route leak
subtitle: A working definition of a BGP route leak and a taxonomy of the kinds that have caused outages.

tldr.problem: Incidents that disrupt Internet routing are commonly called route leaks, but they vary in form and technical detail, so there was no common definition to build solutions on.
tldr.mechanism: The document proposes a working definition, that a route leak is the propagation of routing announcements beyond their intended scope, and then classifies six types of leak by the roles of the network that leaked the route and the network that received it.
tldr.outcome: The result is a shared vocabulary that detection and mitigation work can refer to, built on and extended from earlier work in the IETF.

today: RFC 7908 is an Informational document published in June 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it defines the problem rather than solving it: the document says later work would build detection and mitigation on the definition it gives here.

sections.title: Why a Definition Was Needed
sections.content:
Frequent incidents that result in significant disruptions to Internet routing are commonly called route leaks. Examination of the details of some of these incidents reveals that they vary in their form and technical details. In order to pursue solutions to the route-leak problem, it is important to first provide a clear, technical definition of the problem and enumerate its most common forms.

The document therefore provides a working definition of route leaks, keeping in view many recent incidents that received significant attention, and then enumerates, though not exhaustively, different types of route leak based on observed events on the Internet. It builds on and extends earlier work in the IETF.

The reason the matter needs care is that the same label was applied to events with different causes and different effects. A definition has to be loose enough to cover the incidents that have happened and tight enough to be useful for building detection and mitigation tools.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators had been calling several different kinds of mistake a route leak. Before anyone could build a tool to spot them or prevent them, the community needed to agree on what the words meant.

sections.title: The Working Definition of a Route Leak
sections.content:
The proposed working definition is that a route leak is the propagation of routing announcements beyond their intended scope. That is, an announcement from an Autonomous System (AS) of a learned BGP route to another AS is in violation of the intended policies of the receiver, the sender, and/or one of the ASes along the preceding AS path.

The intended scope is usually defined by a set of local redistribution and filtering policies distributed among the ASes involved. Often these intended policies are defined in terms of the pair-wise peering business relationship between ASes, for example customer, transit provider or peer. A multihomed AS, one connected to more than one upstream provider, has rules about which routes it may pass to which neighbour: routes learned from a transit provider are normally sent to customers and peers, and not to other transit providers.

The result of a route leak can be redirection of traffic through an unintended path, which may enable eavesdropping or traffic analysis, and may or may not result in an overload or a black hole. Route leaks can be accidental or malicious, but most often they arise from accidental misconfigurations.

The definition is not intended to be all-encompassing. The stated aim is a working definition that fits enough observed incidents so that the IETF community has a basis for developing solutions for route-leak detection and mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: A route leak is a network passing on a route it should have kept to itself. Each network has rules about which routes it shares with which neighbour, and a leak breaks one of those rules. The traffic then takes a path nobody planned, which can break connections, slow the network down, or let someone read the traffic.

sections.title: The Common Shape of a Leak
sections.content:
The common form of a route leak occurs when a multihomed customer AS learns a prefix update from one transit provider and leaks the update to another transit provider in violation of intended routing policies. The second transit provider does not detect the leak, and propagates the leaked update to its customers, peers and transit ISPs.

In the figure that illustrates this, ISP1 (AS1) and ISP2 (AS2) are peers of each other, and both are upstream providers for a customer network, AS3. The customer learns the prefix from ISP1 and passes it on to ISP2, and ISP2 spreads it further out. The network that announces a route in violation of the intended policies is referred to in this document as the offending AS.

Once the leak has happened, the damage depends on what the receiving networks do with the announcement. Some will drop it, some will accept it and pass it on, and in the worst case the traffic for the affected prefixes is drawn towards a network that cannot carry it.
sections.plainLanguage: The typical case is a customer with two providers. It learns a route from one, passes it to the other, and the second provider treats it as a real route and spreads it further. The customer is the network that made the mistake, and the document calls it the offending network.

sections.title: The Six Types of Route Leak
sections.content:
Type 1, hairpin turn with full prefix. A multihomed AS learns a route from one upstream ISP and simply propagates it to another upstream ISP, with the turn resembling a hairpin. Neither the prefix nor the AS path in the update is altered. This is similar to a straightforward path-poisoning attack, but with the full prefix, and leaks of this type are often accidental. The leak often succeeds because the second ISP prefers a customer announcement over a peer announcement of the same prefix. Data packets would reach the legitimate destination, albeit via the offending AS, unless they are dropped there because it cannot handle the resulting large volume of traffic. Examples are the Dodo-Telstra incident of March 2012, the VolumeDrive-Atrato incident of September 2014, and the Telekom Malaysia route leak of about 179,000 prefixes, which Level3 accepted and propagated.

Type 2, lateral ISP-ISP-ISP leak. The word lateral here is synonymous with non-transit or peer-to-peer. This type typically occurs when three sequential ISP peers are involved: ISP-B receives a route from ISP-A and in turn leaks it to ISP-C. The typical routing policy between laterally peering ISPs is that they should only propagate to each other their respective customer prefixes. Such leaks are reported by monitoring updates in the global BGP system and finding three or more very large ISPs' AS numbers in sequence in a BGP update's AS path, on the grounds that very large ISPs do not in general buy transit from each other. The detection method also notes exceptions, when one very large ISP does buy transit from another, and makes exceptions for known cases.

Type 3, leak of transit-provider prefixes to peer. The offending AS leaks routes learned from its transit provider to a lateral peer.

Type 4, leak of peer prefixes to transit provider. The offending AS leaks routes learned from a lateral peer to its own transit provider. These leaked routes typically originate from the customer cone of the lateral peer. Examples are the Axcelx-Hibernia leak of Amazon Web Services prefixes, the Hathway-Airtel leak of 336 Google prefixes causing widespread interruption of Google services in Europe and Asia, the Moratel-PCCW leak of Google prefixes, and, in the Dodo-Telstra incident, leaked routes that included routes learned from transit providers as well as lateral peers.

Type 5, prefix re-origination with data path to legitimate origin. A multihomed AS learns a route from one upstream ISP and announces the prefix to another upstream ISP as if it were originating it, stripping the received AS path. This can be called re-origination or mis-origination. Somehow a reverse path to the legitimate origination AS may be present, and data packets reach the legitimate destination albeit via the offending AS; the presence of a reverse path is not attributable to a path-poisoning trick. Sometimes the reverse path is not present, and data packets for the leaked prefix are simply discarded at the offending AS. Examples are the China Telecom incident of April 2010, the GlobalOneBel route leaks of February to March 2013 and May 2013, the Opin Kerfi-Simmin route leaks of July to August 2013, and the Indosat route leak of April 2014. The reverse paths were present in the first three of those and not in the fourth, where the misrouted packets were dropped at Indosat's AS.

Type 6, accidental leak of internal prefixes and more-specific prefixes. An offending AS simply leaks its internal prefixes to one or more of its transit-provider ASes and/or ISP peers. The leaked internal prefixes are often more-specific prefixes subsumed by an already announced, less-specific prefix, and were not intended to be routed in External BGP. The AS receiving those leaks fails to filter them. Such announcements are typically due to transient failures within the AS, so they are short-lived and usually withdrawn quickly. While they last, the more-specific prefixes may be preferred over other aggregate route announcements, redirecting traffic from its normal best path. Leaks of internal routes occur frequently, multiple times in a week, with numbers of prefixes ranging from hundreds to thousands per incident; one conspicuous and widely disruptive leak happened in August 2014, when AS701 and AS705 leaked about 22,000 more-specific prefixes of already-announced aggregates.
sections.plainLanguage: The six types differ in who leaked what to whom. A customer can pass a route from one provider straight to another, or pass a provider's route to a peer, or a peer's route to its provider. A peer-to-peer chain of three networks counts as its own type. One type is worse than the others: the network claims the prefix as its own and hides the path it came by, and then either the traffic still finds its way to the right place or it is dropped.

sections.title: What the Classification Leaves Out
sections.content:
Types 1 through 4 are similar in that a route is leaked in violation of policy in each case, but what varies is the context of the source and destination roles of the leaked route. The document notes that a Type 5 route leak can also happen in conjunction with the relationship contexts of Types 2, 3 and 4. While those possibilities are acknowledged, simply enumerating more types to cover every such special case does not add value as far as solution development is concerned, so those special cases are not included in the enumeration.

The list of types is not meant to be exhaustive either. The taxonomy is meant to cover the forms that have been observed and that concern the Internet user community as well as the network operator community.
sections.plainLanguage: The list covers the common cases rather than every combination. A network that hides the path it learned a route by can also be doing any of the other tricks at the same time, and the document says it is not worth adding a new type for each combination.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states that no security considerations apply, since it is a problem definition document.

The security content that does exist sits in the definition and the taxonomy rather than in a separate section. The definition notes that the result of a route leak can be redirection of traffic through an unintended path that may enable eavesdropping or traffic analysis, and that leaks can be accidental or malicious but most often arise from accidental misconfigurations. The Type 1 description compares the shape of the update to a straightforward path-poisoning attack, with the full prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security section of its own, because it is only defining the problem. The security points are in the definition itself: a leaked route can send traffic past someone who can read it, and a leak can be deliberate or a mistake.

viz.caption: THE SIX TYPES OF ROUTE LEAK (RFC 7908, SECTION 3)

items.label: Hairpin turn with full prefix
items.desc: A multihomed AS learns a route from one upstream ISP and propagates it to another, with neither the prefix nor the AS path altered.

items.label: Lateral ISP-ISP-ISP leak
items.desc: Three sequential ISP peers are involved: ISP-B receives a route from ISP-A and leaks it to ISP-C.

items.label: Transit-provider prefixes to a peer
items.desc: The offending AS leaks routes learned from its transit provider to a lateral peer.

items.label: Peer prefixes to a transit provider
items.desc: The offending AS leaks routes learned from a lateral peer to its own transit provider.

items.label: Prefix re-origination
items.desc: The AS announces the prefix as its own, stripping the received AS path, but a reverse path to the real origin may still exist.

items.label: Internal and more-specific prefixes
items.desc: Internal prefixes, often more-specifics, are leaked to transit providers or peers and are not filtered on receipt.
